title: The daily office
hook: Anglicans pray the Book of Common Prayer morning and evening, with short set prayers called collects

segments.voice: Yesterday, dryness: prayer in a dry and thirsty land. Your line was a dry prayer still counts. Today, prayers with a timetable.

Five thirty on a weekday in an English cathedral. Outside, traffic and buses. Inside, a choir in robes, a dozen people in the old wooden seats, and a service sung there, in some form, for centuries. It's called Evensong. It goes back to 1549, when Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, took the church's daily prayers, in Latin and spread across many services shaped for monks, and put them into English, in two: one for morning, one for evening. He called it the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared: anyone could pray it, at home or in church. Tucked into both services are tiny prayers, a single sentence each. Today's word is their name.

A collect. The stress goes at the front: COLL-ect. It's a short set prayer with a shape: it speaks to God, often recalls something about God, asks for one thing, and closes through Christ. One breath, one request. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from; one old idea is that it collects the silent prayers of everyone present into one sentence. The whole rhythm is called the daily office, from the Latin for duty or service. The habit is older than the church: the Psalms speak of praying "Evening, and morning, and at noon," and Daniel prayed three times a day. Near the end of Evening Prayer comes the collect for aid against all perils, which Cranmer translated from an old Latin night prayer. In the 1662 Book of Common Prayer: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night; for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ. Amen." No streetlights then. Night meant real danger: fire, illness, thieves, the dark itself. People said it before bed, and some still do. Anglicans and Episcopalians pray it, and some Methodists too. Catholics keep their own daily office, the Liturgy of the Hours, and the Orthodox pray Vespers at evening and Matins at morning. Different books, one idea: time marked with prayer, like a heartbeat.

segments.voice: If you pray, say the evening collect slowly: Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night. If you don't pray, let the words pass through you and notice which phrase stays. Then think of one darkness, yours or someone else's, that could use some light tonight, and rest there.

Your line: lighten our darkness. Three old words for when the last light goes off. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Anglicans and Episcopalians pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, at home or in church, ending with set collects; cathedrals often sing Evensong daily, and Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep their own daily hours of prayer.

notes: The 'aid against all perils' collect is generally traced to a Latin Compline collect (Illumina, quaesumus, Domine, tenebras nostras) in the Sarum use. Stated only as 'an old Latin night prayer'. Confirm.
Cranmer's two offices drew on the monastic hours (Matins, Lauds, Prime; Vespers, Compline); 'seven services into two' simplifies (eight hours are sometimes counted). Confirm phrasing.
Origin of the word 'collect' presented as uncertain, with the 'gathering the people's prayers' explanation as one old idea. Confirm.
Evensong 'for centuries': the BCP services were banned during the Commonwealth (1640s–1660), so the phrasing avoids claiming an unbroken run.
The practice repeats a real BCP prayer (not a new prayer). The Methodist mention: Wesley's Sunday Service drew on the BCP; confirm 'many Methodists' is fair.
